mentl/bb038ed:
The lower_scope handler's frame was a 4-tuple
(locals_names, locals_handles, captures_names, captures_handles)
with linear ls_find_str membership scans. Ω.5 consolidates each
frame into one record with six named fields:

  {locals: SortedSet, local_order: List, local_handles: List,
   captures: SortedSet, capture_order: List, capture_handles: List}

Membership upgrades to set_contains (O(log N)) on the sorted name
set; slot index falls back to a linear scan over the insertion-
ordered list ONLY when the name is confirmed present (set_contains
true). The common case (resolve hits) stays sub-linear; the rare
case (negative lookup → fall through to RGlobal) is now O(log N)
instead of O(N).

infer_ctx's stack frames similarly consolidate. The 3-tuple
(row_handle, accumulated_row, fn_span) becomes a record:

  {accumulated_row: EffRow, fn_span: Span, row_handle: Int}

Mutations are explicit reconstructions of the head record per arm —
no functional-update sugar (H2.2) needed; verbose but honest. If
update sugar lands later, the arms collapse to one-line.

Field-sort discipline: records store fields alphabetically (parser
+ mk_record_open invariant). The runtime layout is determined by
that order; Inka source reads via .field — physical layout
irrelevant. Adding a new field is additive — existing code reading
unrelated fields doesn't break (a strict improvement over the prior
tuple-destructure shape, which forced every site to widen).

Renames: ls_find_str → ls_find_in_order. The function's role is
now post-membership-check slot lookup, not membership detection;
the rename marks the new contract.

perennials/bbe0fe4: The guide was not saved after the first visit. DataProvider fires its three fetches from a mount effect at about t=90ms; the service worker does not claim the page until about t=460ms, so on a first visit the data never passed through the Workbox route and never reached Cache Storage. She could open the app at home, watch it work, drive to a field with no signal, and find an empty guide telling her to "open it once where there's signal" -- which is exactly what she had done. Reproduced on fresh profiles, in real airplane mode: one visit gave zero plants; two gave the whole catalogue. The photos hid it, because loading="lazy" fires them after the claim. store.tsx now writes the payloads into the same named cache the SW owns, so one visit is enough. Verified: after ONE visit, airplane mode renders 48 cards. The photo cache was quietly destroying itself. The tags fetched cross- origin with no crossorigin attribute, so the SW stored OPAQUE responses, and Chrome pads each of those by ~7 MB in its storage accounting. Forty-eight photos reported ~400 MB against 1 MB of real webp; the cache then hit the quota and refused every further write, silently, while photos still rendered online -- so offline she would have found the guide only a few dozen pictures deep. The API already sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so one attribute fixes it. But it cannot ship alone: CacheFirst matches on URL, so a CORS request would have been handed the stale opaque entry, failed its check, and painted "no photo" for a plant whose photo was right there. Hence the new cache name and public/sw-purge.js, which deletes the old one on activate. Verified on a simulated upgrade: old cache purged, 48 photos survive, zero broken. 32.5 MB -> 10.2 MB. Also: statuses [200] only, because a no-cors 404 comes back opaque with status 0, matches, and is then served as that plant's photo for six months. purgeOnQuotaError, which is the only self-heal path Workbox has. bits/bb1ceb7:
A bit had one voice, so every mouth flapped to the same sound and two
people could not record their halves separately. A puppet can now have a
take of its own: the bit stays the bed, a puppet without a take still
flaps to it, and one with a take flaps to its own, gated by that take's
span rather than by its passes — the voice is the talker rule for it.

It is recorded against the bit, which plays while the mic is open, and
starts where the playhead was. The panel says whose lines are being said
and suggests headphones. A take can be handed back to the bit, undoably.

It carries through the whole pipeline. Envelopes drive the mouths in the
preview and in the render. The live jam schedules each take alongside the
bed at its own offset and gain, rather than after it — awaiting the bed's
whole decode first would leave every take silent until it finished. The
render mixes each take's PCM into the output buffers, decoded at full
rate, because mixdownMono decimates to 16kHz, which is right for an
envelope and wrong for anything anyone is meant to hear. And a take is
part of the bit file, or a shared bit arrives mute for whoever recorded
it.

The walkthrough gained a real find: a sheet left open silently swallowed
the taps of every later phase, which looked exactly like controls that
did nothing. Taps now check that they will actually land, and say what is
covering them when they will not.

The board is public/tunnel-leaderboard.json, committed to the repo; there
is no server and no database. A qualifying run opens the initials modal in
a GLOBAL variant, then offers a prefilled issue titled
[tunnel-run] AAA 12345. The leaderboard workflow parses the title (env
vars only, nothing interpolated into shell), merges through
scripts/merge-leaderboard.mjs, commits, comments the verdict, closes the
issue, and dispatches deploy.yml explicitly because GITHUB_TOKEN pushes do
not fire on-push workflows. Concurrency serializes racing submissions.

Rules: ties lose, seven-digit cap, exact duplicates rejected, initials
travel with spaces as underscores so title trimming cannot eat them.

The game fetches the board once per mount through refs (the rAF loop never
tears down), shows GLOBAL TOP 10 at game over with the pending run merged
and marked, falls back to the local board offline, and the global champion
becomes the in-game score to beat. Submitting needs a GitHub account;
without one scores stay in localStorage as before.

31 new tests cover title parsing (including injection-shaped titles),
merge and tie rules, fetch normalization, and the issue URL. README
documents the mechanism and corrects the stale PROJECTS path and the
Konami line; the real easter egg is the coin slot.
